statement: In 113 people (the review's table sums to 116) with eye problems after using poppers described in 32 published case reports, case series and conference abstracts (2004 to 2021, pooled in a systematic review searched to November 2021; 108 men, average age 40, more than half reported from the UK), the reports describe a consistent picture: both eyes affected in 67 of 69 with details, with reduced or blurred central vision, flashes and other visual disturbances, or a central blind spot; a yellow spot at the centre of the retina on examination in 53 of 72, and disruption of the layer of light-sensing cells at the centre of the retina on scans in 89 of 111. Use ranged from a single occasion to more than 20 years, and the product was not named for 100 of 113. In those followed up, scans had improved or returned to normal in 46 of 75 (61%), and average sharpness of vision improved from 0.24 to 0.11 logMAR (from about 6/9.5 to about 6/7.5) in 79 eyes of 40 people. With no comparison group and selective follow-up, the reports cannot show how often poppers harm the eyes, which products or patterns of use carry the risk, or how the many people not followed up fared. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Eye doctors in many countries have described people whose central vision became blurry or dim after using poppers, sometimes after a single use, with damage to the light-sensing cells at the centre of the eye; in most of those checked again, the damage got better. These are reports of people who saw an eye doctor, so they cannot tell how often this happens or with which poppers.
population: People with eye problems after recreational poppers use described in 32 published reports (113 patients), 2004 to 2021
exposure: Inhaled poppers (alkyl nitrites; compound named for 13 of 113)
outcome: Symptoms and eye findings at presentation (poppers maculopathy) and change in vision and retinal scans at follow-up
magnitude: Both eyes 67 of 69 (97.1%); complaints (81 in 56 people): acuity changes 36 (44.4%), visual disturbances 29 (35.7%), central scotoma 15 (18.5%); yellow foveal spot 53 of 72 (73.6%); ellipsoid-layer disturbance on OCT 89 of 111 (80.1%); OCT improved or resolved 46 of 75 (61.3%); mean acuity 0.24 to 0.11 logMAR in 79 eyes of 40 people (Wilcoxon Z = −5.800, p < 0.001, eyes treated as independent); 9 of 69 best eyes (13%) at 0.4 logMAR or worse at presentation, 2 followed up, unchanged.

risk_of_bias.note: Published cases only (which cases get published is the main bias here, not rated again under publication bias), exposure self-reported and the product mostly unknown, follow-up selective, and possible double counting across UK series (card sc_bartolo_2023, AMSTAR 2 critically low).

inconsistency.note: Reports from at least 12 countries describe the same picture (Table 1).

indirectness.note: Worded for reported cases, not for everyone who uses poppers.

imprecision.note: Counts of reported cases; denominators uncertain by a few patients (113 in the text, 116 in Table 1).

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim from case reports starts low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias -1 gives very low. Status replicated: 32 independent reports from at least 12 countries, from 2004 onward, describe the same condition after poppers use; the proportions are one pooled description and the review does not tabulate findings report by report. The claim does not say how often poppers damage the eyes, which no source read can show.
